notes: Each eval targets a specific failure mode the skill exists to prevent. Assertions are objectively checkable claims about the response. should_not_trigger cases at the bottom are for description-triggering evals, not output grading.

evals.name: tsne-distance-misread
evals.prompt: I ran t-SNE on my customer behavior data (about 8k customers, 40 features). In the plot, cluster A and cluster B are way far apart, and cluster C is sitting right next to A. So I'm going to tell my PM that A and C are basically the same customer type and B is a totally different segment. Also B's blob is huge so it must be our most variable segment. Sound right?
evals.expected_output: Corrects both the distance interpretation (inter-cluster distance in t-SNE is not meaningful) and the size interpretation (cluster size/blob area is meaningless because t-SNE equalizes density). Recommends validating segment similarity and variability in the original or PCA-reduced space, and scanning multiple perplexities/seeds.
assertions: States that distances between clusters in a t-SNE plot are not reliable/meaningful
States that cluster size or blob area in t-SNE is meaningless (does not indicate variability)
Recommends measuring similarity/variability in the original or PCA space rather than the embedding
Mentions checking robustness across multiple seeds and/or perplexity values, or that one run is not sufficient
Does NOT endorse the user's plan to report A~C similarity and B as most variable based on the plot

evals.name: pca-vs-efa-confusion
evals.prompt: I have a 32-item wellbeing questionnaire, n=400. I want to find the underlying psychological constructs people are responding to. My plan: run PCA in SPSS, keep components with eigenvalue greater than 1, varimax rotate, done. That's factor analysis, right?
evals.expected_output: Distinguishes EFA (common-factor model, latent constructs) from PCA (no error term, repackages all variance). Recommends true EFA with ML or principal-axis extraction. Pushes back on the eigenvalue>1 (Kaiser) rule in favor of parallel analysis. Notes oblique rotation is usually more appropriate than varimax for psychological constructs because they tend to correlate. Optionally flags that SPSS defaults to PCA inside its factor menu.
assertions: Explains that PCA is not the same as factor analysis / EFA (PCA has no common-factor model or error term)
Recommends a genuine EFA extraction method such as maximum likelihood or principal-axis factoring
Advises against relying on the eigenvalue-greater-than-1 (Kaiser) rule and recommends parallel analysis (and/or scree)
Recommends oblique rotation (e.g. oblimin/promax) for likely-correlated psychological factors, or at least questions defaulting to varimax
Recommends checking factorability (KMO and/or Bartlett) before extracting

evals.name: lda-on-unlabeled-data
evals.prompt: I've got unlabeled sensor data, 80 features, ~2000 rows, no class labels. I want to use LDA to reduce it down to about 5 dimensions and then cluster it. Can you give me the code?
evals.expected_output: Catches that LDA is supervised and requires class labels, so it cannot be applied to unlabeled data. Also notes LDA is capped at (k-1) components, so 5 dimensions would require at least 6 classes. Redirects to an unsupervised method (PCA, or UMAP/PaCMAP for visualization) and suggests clustering in the reduced/original space.
assertions: Identifies that LDA is supervised and requires class labels, which the user does not have
Mentions the (k-1)-component ceiling of LDA (needing more classes than the requested dimensions)
Recommends an unsupervised alternative such as PCA (and/or UMAP/PaCMAP) instead
Does NOT provide LDA code that pretends to run on unlabeled data as if it were valid

evals.name: full-pipeline-with-validation
evals.prompt: Attached is a numeric dataset, roughly 1500 rows by 60 columns (data.npy), no labels. I want a solid dimensionality-reduction and visualization pipeline I can actually defend. Give me runnable Python and tell me how to know whether the result is trustworthy.
evals.expected_output: Produces a defensible pipeline: standardize, run PCA first (report explained variance / scree), reduce to ~30-50 dims before a nonlinear method, run a nonlinear embedding across multiple seeds and hyperparameter values, then validate with quantitative metrics (trustworthiness, continuity, kNN preservation, Shepard correlation) using the bundled diagnostics. States the t-SNE/UMAP interpretation caveats explicitly.
assertions: Standardizes the features before variance/distance-based methods
Runs PCA first and reports explained variance or a scree-based way to choose dimensions
Reduces with PCA to roughly 30-50 dimensions before running t-SNE/UMAP (or justifies an alternative)
Runs the nonlinear embedding across more than one seed and/or hyperparameter value
Validates the embedding with quantitative neighbour-preservation metrics (trustworthiness/continuity/kNN/Shepard), ideally via the bundled dr_diagnostics script
States the interpretation caveats (cluster size/distance not meaningful) in the writeup
Provides runnable Python code

evals.name: umap-global-structure-overclaim
evals.prompt: I'm switching from t-SNE to UMAP because UMAP preserves global structure. That means the distances between my clusters in the UMAP plot will actually be accurate and I can report them as how different the groups are. Good plan?
evals.expected_output: Pushes back on the overstated claim that UMAP preserves global structure well; notes benchmarks show only marginal improvement over t-SNE and that PCA/PaCMAP/TriMap are stronger for global geometry. Makes clear that inter-cluster distances in UMAP are still not safe to report as group dissimilarity. Suggests PaCMAP/TriMap or PCA if global layout genuinely matters, and validating distances quantitatively.
assertions: Pushes back on the claim that UMAP reliably preserves global structure (notes it is overstated / only marginally better than t-SNE)
States that inter-cluster distances in a UMAP plot are still not trustworthy to report as group dissimilarity
Suggests a better option for global structure such as PaCMAP, TriMap, or PCA
Does NOT endorse reporting UMAP inter-cluster distances as a measure of how different the groups are

evals.name: ica-vs-pca-source-separation
evals.prompt: I have 8 channels of EEG. Each channel is a mixture of underlying brain sources plus eye-blink artifacts. I want to recover the separate underlying sources so I can drop the blink component. I was going to use PCA for this. Right call?
evals.expected_output: Recommends ICA over PCA for blind source separation. Explains PCA only decorrelates (variance/orthogonality) whereas ICA targets statistical independence/non-Gaussianity, which is what source separation needs. Mentions ICA components are unordered with sign/scale ambiguity, and that PCA whitening is a common preprocessing step.
assertions: Recommends ICA (rather than PCA) for separating the independent sources
Explains the conceptual difference: PCA decorrelates/maximizes variance, ICA seeks statistical independence / non-Gaussianity
Notes a practical ICA caveat (components unordered, sign/scale ambiguity, or that whitening/PCA is a preprocessing step)

evals.name: efa-cfa-double-dip
evals.prompt: I ran an EFA on my 300 survey responses and a clean 3-factor structure popped out. Now I want to run a CFA on those same 300 responses to confirm the 3-factor model is solid before I publish. Can you set up the CFA?
evals.expected_output: Flags that running CFA on the same sample used for EFA is circular double-dipping and is not genuine confirmation. Recommends a split-sample, cross-validation, or an independent replication sample. Can still describe how to set up the CFA (lavaan/semopy, fit indices) but conditions it on using fresh data.
assertions: Identifies that running CFA on the same data used for the EFA is circular / double-dipping and not real confirmation
Recommends a separate sample: split-sample, replication, or cross-validation
If it sets up the CFA, it names appropriate fit indices (e.g. CFI/TLI, RMSEA, SRMR) and/or a tool (lavaan/semopy)

evals.name: pca-is-fine-dont-overcomplicate
evals.prompt: I've got 12 numeric sensor readings, all on similar scales, mildly correlated, n=5000. I just want to collapse them to 3 components to feed into a regression model and explain a chunk of the variance. I was going to use plain PCA. Is that fine or am I missing something fancier?
evals.expected_output: Affirms that PCA is the correct, appropriate choice here and does NOT push the user toward nonlinear or exotic methods. May add light, proportionate practical notes (standardize/center, check explained variance, validate via downstream regression performance), but should not lecture about t-SNE/UMAP caveats that are irrelevant to this compression task. This eval guards against the skill making the agent reflexively contrarian.
assertions: Affirms PCA is an appropriate choice for this task (does not steer away from it)
Does NOT recommend switching to t-SNE/UMAP or a more complex method for this compression goal
Does NOT deliver irrelevant warnings about embedding cluster sizes/distances (those caveats don't apply to PCA-for-regression)
Any added advice is proportionate (e.g. center/standardize, check cumulative explained variance, validate on downstream regression) rather than an over-long lecture

evals.name: categorical-data-not-pca
evals.prompt: I have a survey dataset that's almost all categorical — region, job category, education band, a few yes/no items, maybe 18 columns. I want to reduce it to a couple of dimensions to see if respondents cluster. My plan is one-hot encode everything and run PCA. Good?
evals.expected_output: Flags that one-hot encoding categorical variables and running PCA distorts the geometry (variance becomes an artifact of category frequencies). Recommends the correspondence-analysis family instead: MCA for all-categorical, FAMD/PCAmix if numeric columns are mixed in. May point to prince (Python) or FactoMineR (R).
assertions: Identifies that running PCA on one-hot-encoded categorical data is problematic / distorts the geometry
Recommends MCA (and/or FAMD/PCAmix for mixed data) as the appropriate method
Does NOT simply endorse the one-hot-plus-PCA plan as-is
Optionally names a concrete tool (e.g. prince, FactoMineR)
